walkthroughs.title: Tensor shape, stride, views and copies

steps.excerpt:
def verify():
    # Worked example A: Inspect shape and stride
    x = torch.arange(6, dtype=torch.float64, device="cpu").reshape(2, 3)
    assert (
        tuple(x.shape) == (2, 3)
        and x.stride() == (3, 1)
        and x.device.type == "cpu"
        and x.dtype == torch.float64
    )
steps.title: Worked example A: shape, stride, device and dtype
steps.explanation: torch.arange(6) makes the values 0 to 5, and reshape(2, 3) arranges them as two rows of three. The shape is the logical size. The stride says how many elements to skip in memory to move one step along each axis: 3 to the next row, 1 to the next column. Device and dtype are checked explicitly so nothing is assumed.
steps.observe: stride() returns (3, 1) for a row major 2 by 3 tensor.

steps.excerpt:
# Worked example B: Expose shared storage
    row = x[0]
    row[0] = 99
    assert x[0, 0].item() == 99

    # Worked example C: Create an independent copy
    owned = x.clone()
    owned[0, 0] = -1
    assert owned[0, 0].item() == -1 and x[0, 0].item() == 99
steps.title: Worked examples B and C: views share memory, clones do not
steps.explanation: x[0] is a view of the first row, not a copy. Writing 99 into the view also changes x. clone allocates new memory, so writing -1 into owned leaves x unchanged. .item() converts a one element tensor to a Python number.
steps.observe: Silent writes through views are a common source of bugs.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 4: Trace a transposed layout
    transposed = x.T
    assert (
        tuple(transposed.shape) == (3, 2)
        and transposed.stride() == (1, 3)
        and not transposed.is_contiguous()
    )
    assert transposed.contiguous().is_contiguous()
steps.title: Exercise 4: transposing changes strides, not data
steps.explanation: x.T swaps the axes by swapping the strides to (1, 3). The data is not moved, so the tensor is no longer contiguous in memory. contiguous() makes a compact copy when an operation needs one.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 5: Detect a pairing broadcast
    v = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
    column = v[:, None]
    assert tuple((v - column).shape) == (3, 3) and tuple((v - v).shape) == (3,)

    # Exercise 6: Reject incompatible arithmetic
    try:
        torch.zeros((2, 3)) + torch.zeros(4)
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("incompatible shapes accepted")
steps.title: Exercises 5 and 6: broadcasting and its limits
steps.explanation: v[:, None] turns a length 3 vector into a 3 by 1 column. Subtracting a column from a row broadcasts both to 3 by 3, which is easy to do by accident when you meant elementwise. Shapes (2, 3) and (4,) cannot broadcast, and PyTorch raises RuntimeError.
steps.observe: Check result shapes whenever two tensors meet.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 1: Predict a 3-by-2 layout
    grid = torch.arange(6, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(3, 2)
    assert (
        tuple(grid.shape) == (3, 2)
        and grid.stride() == (2, 1)
        and grid.dtype == torch.float32
        and grid.device.type == "cpu"
    )

    # Exercise 2: Write through a column view
    column = grid[:, 1]
    column[2] = -7
    assert grid[2, 1].item() == -7 and column.stride() == (2,)
steps.title: Exercises 1 and 2: a 3 by 2 grid and a column view
steps.explanation: A 3 by 2 float32 grid has strides (2, 1). grid[:, 1] selects the second column as a view with stride 2, and writing through it changes the grid.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 3: Separate contiguous from clone
    same = grid.contiguous()
    owned = grid.clone()
    same[0, 0] = 100
    owned[0, 0] = -100
    assert (
        same.data_ptr() == grid.data_ptr()
        and grid[0, 0].item() == 100
        and owned[0, 0].item() == -100
    )
    return {"checks": 6, "status": "passed"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(verify())
steps.title: Exercise 3: contiguous may return the same tensor
steps.explanation: When a tensor is already contiguous, contiguous() returns it unchanged, so it shares data_ptr, the memory address. Only clone guarantees independent storage. The script prints the summary after all checks pass.

walkthroughs.title: Multiclass versus multilabel targets and losses

steps.excerpt:
def verify():
    # Exercise 1: Calculate uniform multiclass loss
    logits = torch.zeros((1, 3), dtype=torch.float64)
    target = torch.tensor([1], dtype=torch.long)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        F.cross_entropy(logits, target).item(), np.log(3), atol=1e-12, rtol=0
    )
steps.title: Exercise 1: uniform multiclass loss
steps.explanation: Three equal logits mean softmax assigns probability one third to each class. F.cross_entropy expects raw logits and an integer class index, and returns the negative log of the true class probability, which is log 3 here.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 2: Contrast independent binary outputs
    independent = torch.sigmoid(logits)
    assert independent.tolist() == [[0.5, 0.5, 0.5]] and independent.sum().item() == 1.5
steps.title: Exercise 2: independent sigmoids do not sum to 1
steps.explanation: Applying sigmoid to each logit separately treats each class as its own yes or no question. With all zero logits every output is 0.5, so they sum to 1.5. That is correct for multilabel problems but wrong for picking exactly one class.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 3: Inspect target shapes and types
    classes = torch.tensor([2, 0], dtype=torch.long)
    labels = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]])
    assert (
        tuple(classes.shape) == (2,)
        and tuple(labels.shape) == (2, 3)
        and classes.dtype == torch.long
        and labels.is_floating_point()
    )
steps.title: Exercise 3: target shapes and dtypes
steps.explanation: Multiclass targets are a 1D tensor of long integers, one class per row. Multilabel targets are a 2D float tensor with one 0 or 1 per class. Mixing these up is a common error.
steps.observe: classes has shape (2,) and labels has shape (2, 3).

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 4: Check class-axis normalization
    scores = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0, -2.0], [0.0, 1.0, 3.0]])
    probs = torch.softmax(scores, dim=1)
    torch.testing.assert_close(probs.sum(1), torch.ones(2), atol=1e-6, rtol=0)
steps.title: Exercise 4: softmax along the class axis
steps.explanation: dim=1 normalizes across classes within each row. Using dim=0 would normalize across examples, which is wrong. assert_close checks each row sums to 1 within float32 tolerance.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 5: Name the multilabel denominator
    per_entry = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(
        torch.zeros_like(labels), labels, reduction="none"
    )
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        [per_entry.sum().item(), per_entry.mean().item()],
        [6 * np.log(2), np.log(2)],
        atol=1e-6,
        rtol=0,
    )
steps.title: Exercise 5: the multilabel denominator
steps.explanation: binary_cross_entropy_with_logits with reduction="none" returns one loss per entry. Zero logits give log 2 for each of 6 entries. The sum is 6 log 2 while the mean is log 2, so always state whether a reported loss is summed or averaged.
steps.observe: Different reductions change the scale, not the ranking.

steps.title: Exercise 6: reject an unknown class
steps.explanation: With three classes, valid indices are 0 to 2. Index 3 makes cross_entropy raise, and the test accepts either IndexError or RuntimeError. The script then prints the summary.

walkthroughs.title: Custom modules, buffers and a custom autograd function

steps.title: A residual module with a parameter and a buffer
steps.explanation: Residual subclasses nn.Module. kernel is wrapped in nn.Parameter, so optimizers will train it. register_buffer stores scale as module state that moves with the module and is saved, but is not trained. forward validates input width, then returns x plus a scaled linear transform of x.
steps.observe: With a zero kernel the module returns its input unchanged.

steps.title: A custom autograd function
steps.explanation: Cube defines both directions by hand. forward saves its input with ctx.save_for_backward and returns x cubed. backward receives the gradient flowing in from later layers and multiplies it by the local derivative 3x squared.
steps.observe: The function is called with Cube.apply.

steps.excerpt:
def verify():
    # Worked example A: Build an identity residual
    module = Residual(2)
    x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
    assert torch.equal(module(x), x)
    assert set(dict(module.named_parameters())) == {"kernel"} and set(
        dict(module.named_buffers())
    ) == {"scale"}

    # Worked example B: Keep state stable across calls
    identity = id(module.kernel)
    module(torch.ones((1, 2), dtype=torch.float64))
    assert id(module.kernel) == identity and sum(p.numel() for p in module.parameters()) == 4
steps.title: Worked examples A and B: inspect the state
steps.explanation: named_parameters lists only kernel, while named_buffers lists only scale. Calling the module again must not replace its parameter object, which id() confirms. A 2 by 2 kernel has 4 trainable numbers.
steps.observe: Parameter identity stays stable between calls.

steps.excerpt:
# Worked example C: Check a known residual transform
    with torch.no_grad():
        module.kernel.copy_(torch.eye(2, dtype=torch.float64))
        module.scale.fill_(0.5)
    torch.testing.assert_close(module(x), 1.5 * x, atol=1e-12, rtol=0)

    # Exercise 4: Reject incompatible feature width
    try:
        module(torch.ones((1, 3), dtype=torch.float64))
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("incompatible residual accepted")
steps.title: Worked example C and Exercise 4: set state safely
steps.explanation: torch.no_grad() lets the code overwrite a parameter without recording that edit for gradients. With an identity kernel and scale 0.5 the output is 1.5 times x. A 3 column input is rejected by forward.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 5: Validate a custom cube derivative
    probe = torch.tensor([0.2, -0.7], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    assert torch.autograd.gradcheck(Cube.apply, (probe,), eps=1e-6, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-3)

    # Exercise 6: Inspect the incoming-gradient factor
    value = torch.tensor([2.0], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    (2 * Cube.apply(value)).sum().backward()
    assert value.grad.item() == 24
steps.title: Exercises 5 and 6: check the hand written gradient
steps.explanation: gradcheck compares backward with a numeric estimate using tiny finite differences; float64 is needed for that precision. Multiplying the output by 2 shows the incoming gradient factor: 2 times 3 times 2 squared is 24.

steps.excerpt:
# Exercise 1: Apply a swapping kernel
    swap = Residual(2)
    xs = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
    with torch.no_grad():
        swap.kernel.copy_(torch.tensor([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]], dtype=torch.float64))
        swap.scale.fill_(2.0)
    assert swap(xs).tolist() == [[5.0, 4.0]]

    # Exercise 2: Predict state for a wider module
    wide_residual = Residual(3)
    assert (
        sum(p.numel() for p in wide_residual.parameters()) == 9
        and len(list(wide_residual.buffers())) == 1
    )

    # Exercise 3: Differentiate Cube at a new point
    point = torch.tensor([-1.0], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    (3 * Cube.apply(point)).sum().backward()
    assert point.grad.item() == 9
    return {"checks": 6, "status": "passed"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(verify())
steps.title: Exercises 1 to 3: predict outputs and gradients
steps.explanation: A swapping kernel with scale 2 turns [1, 2] into [1 + 4, 2 + 2]. A width 3 module has 9 parameters and one buffer. At x = -1 with a factor of 3, the gradient is 3 times 3 times 1, which is 9. The script prints the summary.
